lessons.title: Tractor hydraulic systems and components
lessons.html:
Types of tractor hydraulic system

Open-centre systems use a fixed-displacement gear pump. When no valve is operated, oil flows through the open centre of the valves back to the reservoir at low pressure. They are simple and common on smaller tractors, but waste energy because the pump always delivers full flow.

Closed-centre load-sensing (CCLS) systems use a variable-displacement piston pump. A load-sense signal from the working valves tells the pump how much pressure and flow is needed. When nothing is working the pump destrokes and delivers very little flow. These systems are efficient and give precise control, and are found on most mid and large tractors.

Components and what they do

ComponentFunction
Pump (gear, vane, piston)Converts mechanical power to fluid flow
Relief valveLimits maximum system pressure
Directional control valveSends oil to extend or retract an actuator; spools can be detented or float
Flow control valveSets the speed of an actuator
Check valveAllows flow in one direction only
Single-acting cylinderPushed out by oil, returned by load or spring, such as the lift cylinder
Double-acting cylinderPowered both ways, such as loader cylinders
Hydraulic motorTurns flow into rotation, such as on planter fans
AccumulatorStores oil under pressure, for example for ride control or brakes

Three-point hitch control

The rockshaft lifts the lower links. Position control holds the implement at a set height. Draft control senses the pull on the links, through mechanical springs or electronic load pins, and raises or lowers the implement to keep pulling force steady as soil changes. Modern electronic hitch control (EHC) uses sensors and an ECU.

Reading hydraulic symbols

Workshop manuals use ISO hydraulic symbols: circles for pumps and motors, boxes for valve positions with arrows showing flow, and rectangles for cylinders. Learning these symbols lets you trace a circuit on paper before you touch the tractor.

lessons.title: Oil care, pneumatic systems and safe work
lessons.html:
Hydraulic oil: the lifeblood

Most hydraulic failures start with the oil. Oil transmits power, lubricates pumps and valves, carries heat away and seals small clearances.

Contamination

  • Dirt: enters through dirty couplers, breather caps, worn seals and careless top-ups. Fine particles wear pumps and cause valves to stick.
  • Water: from condensation or washing; makes oil milky, causes rust and poor lubrication.
  • Air: from low oil level or suction leaks; causes foaming, noise and spongy operation (cavitation).
  • Heat: from overloading, blocked coolers or relief valves blowing off constantly; breaks down oil.

Prevention: clean quick couplers before connecting and fit dust caps, top up only from clean sealed containers, change filters at the stated hours, keep oil coolers clean, and use the oil specification in the manual. Oil sampling and analysis can show wear metals and contamination before failure.

Pneumatic systems

Tractors that pull heavy trailers on public roads may have air brakes. The engine-driven compressor charges reservoirs through an air dryer and governor or unloader valve. The tractor's brake valve sends a control signal to the trailer through the coupling heads (supply and control lines). On the trailer, a relay or emergency valve applies the brakes if the supply line is lost, so a breakaway trailer stops itself. Spring brakes hold the vehicle when air is lost.

Pneumatic maintenance

  1. Drain water from reservoirs regularly, or check that automatic drains work.
  2. Check the dryer cartridge at the stated interval.
  3. Listen for leaks with the system charged and engine off; use soapy water on fittings.
  4. Check that system pressure builds within the time stated in the manual.

Safe work on fluid power systems

  • Lower all implements and loaders to the ground, stop the engine and cycle the controls to release pressure before opening any line.
  • Accumulators can hold pressure after shutdown; discharge them as the manual shows.
  • Never check for leaks by hand. A hydraulic injection injury needs emergency medical treatment, even if it looks small.
  • Never work under equipment held up only by hydraulics; use mechanical locks or stands.
  • Before disconnecting air lines, chock the wheels because spring brakes may release or apply.

Key points

  • Open-centre systems use fixed pumps; closed-centre load-sensing uses variable pumps.
  • Draft control keeps implement pull steady; position control holds height.
  • Dirt, water, air and heat are the main enemies of hydraulic oil.
  • Trailer air brakes apply automatically if the supply line is lost.
  • Always release pressure and support loads mechanically before working.
